content.text: ts-station-service's own DB spans (`SELECT ts.station`, `SELECT station`) went from sub-millisecond to hundreds of ms, which looks like a database-call fault inside station-service. I'll check the metrics for station-service and mysql, and whether any services were restarted.

input.query: SELECT 'ab' p, service_name, metric, count(*) n, round(avg(value),2) avg_v, round(max(value),2) max_v FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE service_name IN ('ts-station-service','mysql','ts-basic-service') GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'no', service_name, metric, count(*), round(avg(value),2), round(max(value),2) FROM normal_metrics WHERE service_name IN ('ts-station-service','mysql','ts-basic-service') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,3,1

content.text: mysql and basic-service metrics are flat, so the DB slowness isn't a visible resource problem there. Next I'll check restarts and uptime across all services, plus the timing of the station slowdown.

input.query: SELECT 'ab' p, service_name, metric, count(DISTINCT attr_k8s_pod_name) pods, round(min(value),1) mn, round(max(value),1) mx FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE metric IN ('k8s.container.restarts','k8s.pod.uptime') GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'no', service_name, metric, count(DISTINCT attr_k8s_pod_name), round(min(value),1), round(max(value),1) FROM normal_metrics WHERE metric IN ('k8s.container.restarts','k8s.pod.uptime') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,3,1

content.text: No restart changes. Next I'll look at the callers of the slow chain (travel-plan, route-plan, admin-basic-info) and at the time-series of station's DB spans.

input.query: SELECT 'ab' p, service_name, attr_span_kind k, span_name, count(*) n, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,1) p95 FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('ts-travel-plan-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-admin-basic-info-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-admin-route-service') AND attr_span_kind IN ('Client','Server') GROUP BY ALL UNION ALL SELECT 'no', service_name, attr_span_kind, span_name, count(*), round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,1) FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('ts-travel-plan-service','ts-route-plan-service','ts-admin-basic-info-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-admin-route-service') AND attr_span_kind IN ('Client','Server') GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 2,3,1

content.text: The slow path runs station → basic → travel/travel2 → travel-plan/route-plan. Separately, several services (seat, preserve, food, payment, security) have no abnormal spans at all. I'll check whether those services went quiet and whether their pods were replaced.

content.text: Station's DB spans are the only database calls that slowed (p95 ~415 ms vs 0.9 ms normal); every other service's DB calls are unchanged. Now I'll rebuild the caller→callee graph from parent-child span links to see which edges disappeared, including seat's.

input.query: WITH e AS (SELECT 'ab' p, c.trace_id, c.service_name cs, p.service_name ps, c.attr_span_kind ck FROM abnormal_traces c JOIN abnormal_traces p ON c.trace_id=p.trace_id AND c.parent_span_id=p.span_id WHERE c.service_name<>p.service_name UNION ALL SELECT 'no', c.trace_id, c.service_name, p.service_name, c.attr_span_kind FROM normal_traces c JOIN normal_traces p ON c.trace_id=p.trace_id AND c.parent_span_id=p.span_id WHERE c.service_name<>p.service_name) SELECT ps AS caller, cs AS callee, sum(CASE WHEN p='no' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) normal_n, sum(CASE WHEN p='ab' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) abnormal_n FROM e GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 1,2

A second investigator, starting fresh with the same tools, tested the kind of each fault in your draft answer. Their findings:

### `ts-station-service`: you said `database_call_slow`. They conclude `network_loss` (confidence: medium).
Scope: Affected: the ts-station-service database path. Its SELECT and transaction-commit round trips to the database have a slow tail (p95 SELECT 0.4 to 299 ms), and the Server p50 of GET /stations and POST /stations/idlist rises with them. Not affected: the median of the DB calls (SELECT ts.station p50 0.29 to 0.30 ms), the INSERT ts.station calls, and the callers' own spans. Station's own processing is also unchanged, since its time is lost in round trips, not in its code.
Ruled out:
- `database_call_slow`: A steady per-statement slowdown would move the median. SELECT ts.station p25 and p50 stay at 0.3 ms against 0.29 ms normal. Only the tail moves, and the slow durations cluster at about 210, 420, 630 and 850 ms, not a steady amount. Commit and save slow too, not just one statement. INSERT ts.station is normal (0.2 ms), though with only 3 abnormal samples.
- `network_delay`: Delay moves the 25th, 50th and 95th percentiles together by hundreds of ms. Here p25 and p50 of the station DB calls are flat, and only the tail moves, so it is not a uniform added latency.
- `application_method_slow`: The slow time sits in Internal spans that wrap DB round trips (Transaction.commit p50 207 ms, StationRepository.save, findByNames), and the DB Client spans themselves are fast at the median. The step pattern in those DB round trips points to the link, not a method's own execution. I did not compute self-time for each method, so this rejection is moderate.
- `network_partition`: Calls succeed: the station DB spans complete with durations in the 200 to 3300 ms range, and the Server spans still answer. Partition would show failed or timed-out calls, and the error share for the station calls is 0.00 both normal and abnormal. It is in the same equivalence class as network_loss anyway.
Evidence:
- Slow durations on the station's DB-related spans cluster at about 210, 420, 630 and 850 ms, with many SELECT ts.station spans in the 210 ms bucket (84) and Transaction.commit in 210 ms (10). Steps near 200 ms are the signature of TCP retransmission timeouts, consistent with network loss on the link rather than a steady slowdown.
  `SELECT span_name, attr_span_kind, round(duration/1e6,-1) AS bucket_ms10, count(*) AS n FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-station-service' AND (span_name IN ('SELECT ts.station','Transaction.commit','StationRepository.findAll','StationRepository.findByNames','StationRepository.save')) AND duration>50e6 GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 1,3`
- Abnormal SELECT ts.station Client spans (n=633): p25 0.3 ms, p50 0.3 ms, p95 298.9 ms. The median is unchanged from normal (0.29 ms), so the calls are not uniformly slower; only the tail moved, which rejects database_call_slow and network_delay.
  `SELECT span_name, round(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.25)/1e6,1) AS p25, round(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.5)/1e6,1) AS p50, round(quantile_cont(c.duration,0.95)/1e6,1) AS p95, count(*) AS n FROM abnormal_traces c WHERE c.service_name='ts-station-service' AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' AND c.span_name LIKE 'SELECT%' GROUP BY 1`
- Normal vs abnormal for station spans: SELECT ts.station Client p50 0.29 to 0.32 ms and p95 0.4 to 298.9 ms (n 997 to 633); Transaction.commit Internal p50 0.23 to 206.9 ms and p95 1.6 to 845.2 ms; StationController.query Server-side Internal p50 2.3 to 430 ms; INSERT ts.station p50 0.19 to 0.18 ms. Slowness is confined to a subset of DB round trips, while the Server spans of the callers from basic-service and admin-basic-info-service absorb the delay.
  `SELECT span_name, attr_span_kind, count(*) AS n, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.5)/1e6,2) AS p50_ms, round(quantile_cont(duration,0.95)/1e6,1) AS p95_ms FROM normal_traces WHERE service_name='ts-station-service' GROUP BY 1,2 (run as the combined normal/abnormal comparison on ts-station-service spans)`

### `ts-seat-service`: you said `pod_unavailable`. They agree (confidence: low).
Scope: Affected: ts-seat-service's traffic. In the incident window it emits no spans, and no caller makes a traced call to it; the normal-period left_tickets calls from ts-travel-service, ts-travel2-service and ts-travel-plan-service (140, 60 and 44 per period) are absent, and its own outgoing calls to config and order stop. Not affected: the seat pod itself. Its uptime runs continuously across the boundary with no restart, its memory and network I/O stay at normal levels, and its metrics keep arriving. Callers' traffic is redistributed rather than failing: travel POSTs move to basic and route-plan, and no caller span in the incident is an error or timeout. The claimed pod_unavailable is only weakly supported, because the seat container looks alive; I report it at low confidence as the least-contradicted kind, not as a clean finding.
Ruled out:
- `network_partition`: A cut connection makes callers' Client spans fail at once or hang to a timeout. Every abnormal caller POST has zero error status (travel-service 313 POSTs, 0 errors; travel2 303, 0 errors), and no abnormal Client span to seat exists at all. Network partition and network loss are one equivalence class, so loss is rejected on the same ground.
- `network_delay`: Delay would slow every call on the connection while calls still complete. Calls to seat are absent in the incident rather than slower, and no seat-bound Client span exists to measure.
- `http_aborted`: Aborted HTTP exchanges would show error-status Client spans on seat routes. In the incident there are no seat-route Client spans and no error-status caller spans.
- `http_slow`: Slow HTTP requests would produce Client spans on seat routes with raised durations. None exist in the incident; the normal seat route latency (left_tickets Server p50 7.2 ms) cannot be compared to a slowed one.
- `dns_lookup_failed`: A name-resolution failure would leave caller spans with name-resolution errors before any connection attempt. Logs are empty for every service in both periods, and caller spans show no error status, so there is no DNS signature.
- `container_memory_saturated`: Seat container memory stays at about 455 MB (abnormal average 455,208,550 against normal 455,103,147), and pod memory at about 483 MB in both periods. There is no memory squeeze.
- `container_cpu_saturated`: Seat container and pod CPU usage are about 0.001 in the incident and 0.012 normal, so there is no CPU saturation.
- `process_cpu_saturated`: JVM recent CPU utilization is about 0.001 in the incident against 0.009 normal, so the process is not CPU-bound.
- `pod_failure`: A kill and restart would show a uptime reset or a new pod name with a gap, and restarts would rise. Seat uptime is one pod across both periods (normal ends 12:01:14, abnormal starts 12:01:24, values continue), and no restart appears, so the pod was not restarted.
- `application_exception`: Seat-side error spans or exceptions would appear in seat's own traces or logs. Seat has no spans at all in the incident, and logs are empty in both periods, so there is no exception evidence.
- `database_call_slow`: Seat has no spans in the incident to show a database call's time; the seat-side database call pattern cannot be measured, so this is rejected only for lack of any seat-side span evidence.
Evidence:
- Seat's own spans: none in the abnormal period, while the normal period has Server left_tickets (384), Client GET config (384) and Client POST (417) spans. Seat is silent in traces during the incident.

- Travel, travel2 and travel-plan POSTs to ts-seat-service: 44, 140 and 60 normal (no travel-plan to seat pairs in the incident). In the incident, travel-service POSTs go to ts-basic-service (155), travel2 to ts-basic-service (214), and travel-plan to ts-route-plan-service (146, against 26 normal). Calls are redistributed, not failing.
  `WITH allt AS (SELECT 'ab' per, * FROM abnormal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'nm', * FROM normal_traces) SELECT c.per, c.service_name caller, s.service_name callee, count(*) n FROM allt c JOIN allt s ON s.trace_id=c.trace_id AND s.parent_span_id=c.span_id AND s.attr_span_kind='Server' AND s.per=c.per WHERE c.attr_span_kind='Client' AND c.service_name IN ('ts-travel-plan-service','ts-travel-service','ts-travel2-service') AND c.span_name='POST' GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY 2,1,3`
- Caller POST Client spans in the incident carry zero error status (travel-service 313, travel2 303, travel-plan 267 with 0 errors), so there are no failed calls to seat to read as a partition.
  `SELECT 'ab' per, service_name, attr_span_kind, count(*) n, sum(CASE WHEN attr_status_code='Error' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) errs FROM abnormal_traces WHERE service_name IN ('ts-travel-service','ts-travel2-service','ts-travel-plan-service') AND attr_span_kind='Client' AND span_name='POST' GROUP BY 1,2,3`
- Seat uptime is a single continuous series: normal 46 samples averaging 425.7 s, abnormal 20 samples averaging 739.3 s, with no reset. Restarts show no change, so there was no kill and restart.
  `SELECT per, metric, count(*) n, round(avg(value),3) avgv, round(min(value),3) minv, round(max(value),3) maxv FROM (SELECT 'ab' per, metric, value FROM abnormal_metrics_sum WHERE service_name='ts-seat-service' UNION ALL SELECT 'nm', metric, value FROM normal_metrics_sum WHERE service_name='ts-seat-service') WHERE metric IN ('k8s.pod.uptime','k8s.container.restarts') GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 2,1`
- Seat container memory (455.2 M against 455.1 M normal), pod memory (483.5 M against 483.3 M) and CPU (0.001 against 0.012) are flat, and network I/O stays at its normal level (31.3 M against 28.6 M average). The container is alive, which argues against an instance that is gone.
  `SELECT per, metric, count(*) n, round(avg(value),3) avgv FROM (SELECT 'ab' per, metric, value FROM abnormal_metrics WHERE service_name='ts-seat-service' UNION ALL SELECT 'nm', metric, value FROM normal_metrics WHERE service_name='ts-seat-service') WHERE metric IN ('container.memory.usage','k8s.pod.memory.usage','container.cpu.usage','k8s.pod.network.io') GROUP BY 1,2 ORDER BY 2,1`

Its SELECT and transaction-commit round trips to the database have a slow tail (p95 SELECT 0.4 to 299 ms), and the Server p50 of GET /stations and POST /stations/idlist rises with them. Not affected: the median of the DB calls (SELECT ts.station p50 0.29 to 0.30 ms), the INSERT ts.station calls, and the callers' own spans. Station's own processing is also unchanged, since its time is lost in round trips, not in its code.

ruled_out.why: A steady per-statement slowdown would move the median. SELECT ts.station p25 and p50 stay at 0.3 ms against 0.29 ms normal. Only the tail moves, and the slow durations cluster at about 210, 420, 630 and 850 ms, not a steady amount. Commit and save slow too, not just one statement. INSERT ts.station is normal (0.2 ms), though with only 3 abnormal samples.
Delay moves the 25th, 50th and 95th percentiles together by hundreds of ms. Here p25 and p50 of the station DB calls are flat, and only the tail moves, so it is not a uniform added latency.

The slow time sits in Internal spans that wrap DB round trips (Transaction.commit p50 207 ms, StationRepository.save, findByNames), and the DB Client spans themselves are fast at the median. The step pattern in those DB round trips points to the link, not a method's own execution. I did not compute self-time for each method, so this rejection is moderate.

Calls succeed: the station DB spans complete with durations in the 200 to 3300 ms range, and the Server spans still answer. Partition would show failed or timed-out calls, and the error share for the station calls is 0.00 both normal and abnormal. It is in the same equivalence class as network_loss anyway.

**Verdict: the evidence does not support `database_call_slow`. It points to a network fault on the link between `ts-station-service` and its database, most likely network_loss (equivalent to network_partition under the scoring rules, though a partition is less likely here because calls succeed). Confidence is moderate.**

**Why `database_call_slow` fails**

- **The median of the DB calls did not move.** Station's `SELECT ts.station` Client spans have p25 = p50 = 0.3 ms in the incident, against 0.29 ms normal. Only the tail moved (p95 0.4 → 299 ms). A steady per-statement slowdown would move the median too.
- **The slowness is not in the DB calls at all for most of the affected requests.** `GET /stations` has a Server p50 of 431 ms, but its DB Client spans have a median of 0.3 ms. The time sits in the Internal spans above the DB calls: `Transaction.commit` (p50 207 ms, normal 0.23 ms), `StationRepository.save` and `StationRepository.findByNames`.
- **Other statements and transactions on the same connection are also affected.** `Transaction.commit` and `StationRepository.save` are slow, and `INSERT ts.station` looks normal (0.2 ms), though it has only 3 abnormal samples, so that is weak evidence.

**What the distribution shows**

The slow durations of the DB-related spans cluster at roughly 210, 420, 630 and 850 ms. For example, 84 `SELECT ts.station` spans fall in the 210 ms bucket, and `Transaction.commit` and `findByNames` show the same steps. Steps at multiples of about 200 ms are the signature of TCP retransmission timeouts, which is the loss/corruption shape: most calls stay fast, and a tail appears in 200 ms steps. Irregular, steady, per-statement slowdowns do not produce this pattern.

**Limits**

- Loss and corruption cannot be told apart from these traces, and I cannot confirm the cause on the mysql side. The `hubble_*` per-connection metrics are not recorded for this case.
- I did not check whether station's pod or mysql showed resource pressure. That would be the next step if the lead wants to rule out a server-side cause, since the 200 ms steps could also come from something other than the network.

**Verdict: `pod_unavailable` is not supported as stated. I'd put low confidence on any single kind here, and I would not accept the claim without further evidence.**

**What supports it.** Seat emitted no spans in the incident window (327/min to 0), and no caller made a traced call to it. The normal-period `left_tickets` calls from travel, travel2 and travel-plan (140 + 60 + 44 per period) are absent in the incident. Seat's own outgoing calls to config and order also stop.

**On the other kinds.** A partition or loss would leave Client spans with errors or long durations, and none exist, so the network kinds are not supported either. Seat's own latency does not change where it is still answering, so an in-process slowdown is not the explanation. The evidence does not fit any of the listed kinds cleanly.

**Caveat.** The seat-side facts show a live container that stopped receiving traffic and stopped making calls, with no restart. That is closer to "traffic stopped reaching seat" than to "seat instance gone". Whether that is `pod_unavailable` depends on the GT-side cutoff, which the equivalence class leaves unresolved. I would not rely on the lead's zero-span evidence alone; it is the same observation from the caller's side.
